headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when Langflow ingests or routes content from the static awesome-selfhosted list.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is a content source, while Langflow can chain agents and ingest files or flow inputs. If the list content is fed into a flow, Langflow may treat attacker-controlled text as instructions. The pathway is plausible in default deployments, but the blast radius is limited to the flow context rather than direct system compromise.
conditions: IF awesome-selfhosted content is copied into a Langflow flow node or uploaded file
IF Langflow components parse that content as instructions or prompts
mitigations: Add a prompt-delimiter wrapper around imported text
Require a human review step before any flow executes imported content
Disable automatic prompt chaining for untrusted text
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all imported list entries

B_data_leakage.rationale: Langflow has broad network egress and can read/write the server filesystem, while awesome-selfhosted is a knowledge-management source that may be used to curate or route sensitive notes. If sensitive material is placed into Langflow flows, it can be sent to model providers or arbitrary HTTP services. The pair does not prove leakage by itself, but the default exposure is meaningful.
conditions: IF sensitive notes or documents from awesome-selfhosted are uploaded into Langflow
IF a flow calls external model providers or HTTP services with that content
mitigations: Restrict Langflow flows to local-only providers
Remove sensitive documents from shared flow inputs
Turn off external HTTP tools in production flows
requires-engineering: enforce per-flow data classification filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is non-runnable and has no write surfaces, but Langflow can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses. The pair therefore does not create a direct write-write conflict, yet Langflow's mutable server state can still collide with any shared workspace used to store the list or generated artifacts. Uncertainty about deployment isolation pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents are deployed against the same writable workspace
IF Langflow flows write artifacts into directories also used for the list source
mitigations: Place the list source in a read-only directory
Separate Langflow output directories from source repositories
Run one flow instance per workspace
requires-engineering: add file-locking around shared artifacts

D_cascading_error.rationale: Langflow can chain multiple agents and wire tools into flow nodes, so it may treat upstream content as authoritative unless the flow explicitly verifies it. awesome-selfhosted can supply curated entries that downstream flows may render or act on. This is a plausible default interaction path, but not enough evidence for high because no direct action-taking workflow is shown.
conditions: IF a Langflow flow uses awesome-selfhosted entries as upstream context
IF downstream nodes act on those entries without validation
mitigations: Insert a verification node before any action-taking step
Require citations for every imported entry
Mark imported content as untrusted in the flow UI
requires-engineering: add schema validation between nodes

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, residency, or retention mismatch is evidenced in the profiles. awesome-selfhosted is a public open-source list, and Langflow's documented data classes are flow inputs and intermediate outputs. The only plausible compliance issue is if operators place regulated data into Langflow, which is an unusual configuration rather than a default breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into Langflow flows
IF the deployment stores those secrets or outputs outside the required retention policy
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in flows
Review Langflow secret storage settings
Set short retention on flow logs
requires-engineering: add residency controls per tenant
